  --  in other words, the beneficiary of people who die early are the people who live long.

  --  which means that individual accounts are impractical since you cannot segregate out from a collective asset pool any amount that might "belong" to one particular person.

That being said, the most sensible reform is to adjust retirement age to life expectancy at retirement.

Such “blow-ups” occur mainly on older, heavily stressed or previously damaged concrete pavements; they are considered unlikely on modern concrete roads. Subsequent recounts have more than doubled that number after 7,000 new islands it didn't know existed were discovered.  For the recount, geographers used advanced mapping technology and cross-referenced with past aerial photos.  The big picture is that all weather is now affected by global warming. Natural variability of course still happens. For every 1C warming there is about 7% more atmospheric moisture. 

But ironically, an atmosphere that can hold more moisture also means it sucks plants and soils dry, even when there isn't a drought, other than when there's precipitation. That's what's happening especially in the U.S. West. Most of the wildfires there are ignited by dry lightening. 

To understand how climate change is affecting different areas of the U.S. lower 48 states, and at different times of the year, I highly recommend this article.

  "Climate Change: A Tale of Two Americas",  at Open Mind blog - Word Press

Unfortunately, some service people self harm because they cannot stand these strains; that is true across nearly all large-scale deployments. Should the Navy have better maintenance and life support performance? Yes, and that is a long-running problem exacerbated by inadequate available vessels and manpower to meet constant rotational combat and noncombatant deployments. This is just as much a problem of shipbuilding, budgets, and global commitments as it is a narrow issue with the Iran War deployments. And perhaps it also reflects on some morale and professionalism issues within the naval service. I'm an appellate lawyer. At an ABA Appellate Summit meeting maybe 15 years ago, Justice Thomas explained to attendees his approach to questioning.

When he was a baby lawyer in Missouri, he nervously prepared for his first appellate argument, worrying about what tough questions he'd get from the court. But the judges on the court allowed him to make his argument without a single interruption. He was so grateful to them that, when he became a jurist, he resolved to treat lawyers that way. That's why he didn't interrupt lawyers at the lectern for years; he figured he was being kind to us.

I'll fast-forward and turn from history to inference: When SCOTUS adopted the current your-turn-next setup in 2020, he asked questions like any other member of the Court. That's because he wasn't interrupting anyone; this was his time, set aside for him.

The irony of this is that every experienced appellate advocate earnestly *wants* to be interrupted. We want to know what's bothering Justice X about our argument, so we can address it. One of the difficulties in determining Zhu's role is that many foreign academics as well as Western bankers and investment managers lauded him unduly, ascribing an influence and power that never resembled reality. Zhu himself complained that his ability to see many reforms and policy initiatives through was limited by local officials and even by President Jiang Zemin, who Zhu rightly saw as only too eager to secure political support for his own agenda. Tensions between Zhu and Jiang persisted for years, beginning in Jiang taking credit for keeping Shanghai stable in 1989, and hardly crediting Zhu's yeoman work behind the scenes. Zhu was also sent to deal with the sit-down protests by a certain religious cult in Beijing in 1999, and reportedly told aides that he believed that he was being set-up to take the fall if matters went sideways. 

Those were complex days in Chinese politics. There's every reason to believe that the same dynamics of debate and disagreement in the Chinese leadership are still present. But given the current atmosphere outside China--that is, the dearth of financial support for Chinese studies and the absence of any commitment by governments and universities to devote resources to new thinking and new thinkers--we may never know.

The NYPD put Habib on probation several years ago after he was caught on camera putting another person in a chokehold. He has also been disciplined in other cases for using excessive force and making offensive comments, according to police watchdog records. 

Habib and several other officers crowded into the back of an ambulance where Nyamaah was being treated for cuts to his hand, according to Naughton and body camera footage played at trial. 

As Habib and the other officers tried to handcuff Nyamaah and arrest him for criminal mischief, Habib wrapped his arm around the man’s neck, squeezing so tight that the veins in his bicep pulsed and Nyamaah lost consciousness, according to the DA’s office. Naughton said during opening statements that the chokehold was “unprovoked,” “unnecessary” and “unjustified.” 

Fellow officers who were with Habib the night he used the chokehold also testified at trial that they knew the tactic violated NYPD policy. They said they spoke with a union representative when they got back to the precinct and had planned to report Habib’s actions until they found out that he had already notified a supervisor himself.

The first was with my new SLR camera using Kodak Plus-X B&W film and homemade solar filters from fogged film (state-of-the-art back then!).  I didn't know enough to remove the filter during totality, so the total shots were blank but the partial shots were terrific.

The second was using my cheapo Canon Powershot digital camera, using homemade filters using mylar solar filter sheets.  This worked much better and I knew to remove the filters for totality.  I switched to video mode for the final few minutes before totality so I have sound, too.

Gotta say, the best part is people's reactions as the sun goes out in the middle of the day.  For the first one someone nearby kept chickens and the rooster crowed.

Living down in the Lower 48, I find I often take basic services like electricity and heating for granted. Flip a switch, and there they are. But whenever I visit Alaska, I’m struck by how difficult and expensive all those modern conveniences can be in a place that is potentially so dangerous without them. 

I went to Manley Hot Springs to understand Alaska’s rural energy crisis and left with a new appreciation for how easy I have it.

comments.name: Don Vito
comments.body:
The “war” with Iran has upended not only Alaskans but many others with the higher costs of fuel that affects much of everything we take for granted.

Alaska is unique that much of the fuel for their daily needs relies on imports-diesel refined in other countries to meet demand or the crude can only be refined in refineries in other countries.

In my state of residence it is reported that the state is self-sufficient in crude production and distillate refining.
But, our oil prices are tethered to the commodities casino whose players determine the price of crude at the well head or loading facility.

One would ask, if the United States is the largest producer of crude then why is the country subject to the commodities casino in which the pricing affects all, and in particular those remote communities in Alaska-along with our other states and territories that rely on fuel oil or diesel?  Trump asked that question-and this is possibly the few times I agree with him.

Sadly, these prices will linger for years should the “war” be resolved.
